name: Reactive Arthritis

ethnicAssociations: More common in populations with high HLA-B27 prevalence
Post-chlamydial form more common in males; post-enteric form equal sex distribution

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: No universally accepted formal criteria; clinical diagnosis based on temporal association with preceding infection

criteria.description: Preceding symptomatic infection (urogenital or enteric) 1-4 weeks before arthritis onset
Laboratory evidence of preceding triggering infection (culture, serology, PCR)
Mucocutaneous lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagica, circinate balanitis, oral ulcers)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Typical asymmetric oligoarthritis with evidence of or history of preceding infection (urogenital or enteric) within 1-4 weeks. Exclusion of other causes of arthritis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Common triggering organisms: Chlamydia trachomatis, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter. The classic triad of arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis occurs in only a minority of patients.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Asymmetric oligoarthritis following infection (typically lower extremity)
pathognomonic.notes: Knees, ankles, and feet most commonly affected; onset 1-4 weeks post-infection

common.notes: May be initial trigger or part of reactive process

occasional.notes: Hyperkeratotic skin lesions on palms and soles; can mimic pustular psoriasis
Painless shallow erosions on glans penis
More common in chronic/recurrent disease and HLA-B27+ patients

rare.notes: Very rare; seen in chronic cases

laboratory: Elevated ESR and CRP during acute phase
HLA-B27 positive in 50-80% of patients (predicts severity and chronicity)
Urethral swab or first-void urine NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis
Stool culture for enteric pathogens (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter)
imaging: Radiographs often normal early in disease
Entheseal calcification (Achilles, plantar fascia) in chronic cases
Sacroiliac joint imaging may show asymmetric sacroiliitis
MRI: bone marrow edema at entheses and sacroiliac joints
genetic: HLA-B27 associated with increased risk and severity
Not a single-gene disorder; polygenic susceptibility
other: Careful sexual and travel/food history for triggering infection
Joint aspiration to exclude septic arthritis and crystal arthropathy

distinguishingFeatures: PsA has psoriatic skin plaques (not keratoderma blennorrhagica)
AS has insidious onset without infectious trigger
AS is chronic and progressive from onset
hEDS has generalized hypermobility without inflammatory arthritis

redFlags: Acute monoarthritis with crystals on polarized microscopy (gout/pseudogout)
Chronic recurrent course (>6 months) suggesting evolution to chronic SpA
HIV risk factors (reactive arthritis can be severe and treatment-resistant in HIV)
references: Selmi C, Gershwin ME. Diagnosis and classification of reactive arthritis. Autoimmun Rev. 2014;13(4-5):546-9.
Carter JD, Hudson AP. Reactive arthritis: clinical aspects and medical management. Rheum Dis Clin North Am. 2009;35(1):21-44.
Hannu T. Reactive arthritis. Best Pract Res Clin Rheumatol. 2011;25(3):347-57.
Schmitt SK. Reactive arthritis. Infect Dis Clin North Am. 2017;31(2):265-77.
